newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solvay a 'buy' despite dull 1996 - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Solvay a 'buy' despite dull 1996 - analysts.

text.p: Shares in Belgian chemicals and drugs company Solvay are a 'buy' again after a recent five percent correction, a view analysts also defend by pointing to the group's prospects in the week it is due to publish results.
Solvay stock closed at 22,275 francs on Monday, up just over half a percent, and outperforming the Bel-20 share index .BFX which ended at 2,053.51 points, up only 0.1 percent.

The correction, which took the share down to 22,150 francs on Friday, eroded only a part of the 20 percent rise since the start of the year. The Bel-20 gained just under 10 percent since the start of 1997 trading year on January 2.
"From about 19,375 the share has been a 'buy'," a trader at a Belgian brokerage said.
At just 24,000 francs a selling point would have been reached, he added, pointing to the share's 12-month high of 23,925.
His caution was in part inspired by the fact that Solvay's current product mix makes it sensitive to cyclical swings. He noted chemicals prices had slipped in 1996 after a good 1995.
"They have swung back up again now and forecasts are for a peak in earnings in 1997 or 1998," he said. "You should consider buying now with a view to that."
One analyst pointed out that the size of the group and the diversity of activities meant that "disappointing results in one division could be offset by improvements in others."

Analysts expected uninspiring 1996 results from Solvay. Earnings per share forecasts hover around 1,412 francs, down from 1,471 francs in 1995, but 1997 should see an encouraging rise in EPS to 1,750 francs.
Dividend might be held steady at 550 francs per share, or nudge up to 565, for 1996 before a clear rise in 1997 to 600 francs in 1997, they said.
"With those (1996) results the share could come under pressure...but soon again people will refocus on the important role Solvay is assigning to its drugs sector," one said.

"In the longer run, in two to three years, pharmaceuticals will become more important," said broker Damien Crispiels at Bank Degroof in Brussels, noting drugs currently accounted for about 15 percent of sales and earnings before interest and tax (EBIT).
Total sales in 1995 were $9.3 billion. Human health sales amounted to 34 billion Belgian francs ($1.16 billion).
Analysts said improved results of Solvay's pharmaceutical products would not show through in the short term. Solvay is developing two or three drugs against schizophrenia and anxiety.
Solvay has said it would spend the proceeds from the sale of its animal health businesses on acquiring human pharmaceutical product lines or companies in the U.S.
It sold its animal health businesses to American Home Products Corp for 14 billion francs ($448.8 million), netting it a pre-tax capital gain of around six billion francs.
Together with a one billion Deutsche mark bank credit line the group has around one billion dollars at its disposal.

Solvay's share of the pharmaceuticals market in Europe was more than one percent in 1995. In the U.S., where it has only 0.3 percent, it is looking for fast growth. It has said it is not aiming for volume, but for "big and growing" profits.

Solvay has said it expects 1996 earnings to be on par with those of 1995 despite a 28 percent drop of first-half profit. Full-year results would depend mainly on economic development in Europe, where the group realises two thirds of its sales.
